summary: Revelation 3 (22 verses) continues the story of lamb and dragon. Starting with '“And to the angel of the assembly in Sardis write: “He who has the seven Spirits of God and the seven stars says these things: “I know your works, that you have', it moves through themes of lamb and dragon, victory and calls readers toward new creation.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows lamb and dragon lived out in patmos, persecution. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

questions.question: What is happening in Revelation 3?
questions.answer: In 22 verses, this chapter revelation 3 (22 verses) continues the story of lamb and dragon. starting with '“and to the angel of the assembly in sardis write: “he who has the seven spirits of god and the seven stars says these things: “i know your works, that you have', it moves through themes of lamb and dragon, victory and calls readers toward new creation. The setting is patmos, persecution, written to seven churches in asia. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote Revelation and why 3 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally john, addressed to seven churches in asia around ad 90-95. This chapter fits the book's purpose as apocalypse + letters — its themes of lamb and dragon, victory build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'faith' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: Trust, loyalty to God. In this chapter, it appears in context of lamb and dragon. For a first-time reader: think of it as trust, loyalty to god, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through lamb and dragon and victory, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 12 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'He who overcomes, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God, and he will go out from there no more. I will write on him the name of my God and the name of the city of my God...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about lamb and dragon. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
